title: Study of Compounds: Nitric Acid
tagline: Study the preparation, properties and reactions of nitric acid as an acid and oxidising agent.

overview.intro: Nitric acid (HNO3) is an important mineral acid known for its strong acidic nature and powerful oxidising properties. In the laboratory it is prepared from nitrates using concentrated sulphuric acid, while industrially it is manufactured by the Ostwald process. This chapter examines preparation, physical and chemical properties, reactions with metals and non-metals in different conditions, and tests for nitrates, with emphasis on observations and balanced equations.

facts.label: Key character
facts.value: Strong acid and strong oxidising agent

learningOutcomes: Describe laboratory preparation and collection of nitric acid.
Explain physical properties and why pure nitric acid is stored carefully.
Describe chemical properties including acidic and oxidising behaviour.
Compare reactions of dilute and concentrated nitric acid with metals and non-metals.
Identify tests for nitric acid and nitrates such as the brown ring test.

blocks.text: In the laboratory, nitric acid is prepared by heating potassium nitrate or sodium nitrate with concentrated sulphuric acid in a glass retort. Nitric acid vapours are produced and condensed to a liquid: KNO3 + H2SO4(conc.) → KHSO4 + HNO3↑ (at temperatures below 200°C). The apparatus is all-glass because nitric acid vapours attack cork and rubber.

Industrially, nitric acid is manufactured by the Ostwald process from ammonia. Ammonia is catalytically oxidised to nitric oxide, which is further oxidised to nitrogen dioxide and absorbed in water in presence of oxygen to form nitric acid. The process highlights the link between ammonia and nitric acid production.

items: Use concentrated sulphuric acid as a non-volatile acid to displace nitric acid.
Keep temperature controlled to avoid decomposition and unwanted products.
Collect distillate in a cooled receiver; apparatus must be glass.
Pure nitric acid is colourless but may turn yellow on standing due to decomposition.

blocks.text: Pure nitric acid is a colourless, fuming liquid with a pungent smell. It is miscible with water and highly corrosive. On exposure to light or heat, it decomposes partially to nitrogen dioxide, oxygen and water, giving a yellowish colour: 4HNO3 → 4NO2 + 2H2O + O2. This is why nitric acid is stored in dark or brown bottles.

Concentrated nitric acid is a strong oxidising agent, and its reactions often differ from those of typical dilute acids. Fuming nitric acid contains dissolved nitrogen dioxide and is especially reactive. Careful handling and appropriate storage conditions are necessary to maintain purity and safety.

items.meaning: Concentrated nitric acid containing dissolved NO2, giving brown fumes.
Breakdown of a compound into simpler substances, as nitric acid does on heating or in light.
Industrial method for manufacturing nitric acid from ammonia.

learn.title: Chemical Properties: Acidic and Oxidising Behaviour

blocks.text: Dilute nitric acid behaves as a strong acid, reacting with bases, carbonates and some metals to form nitrates. However, unlike dilute hydrochloric or sulphuric acid, it usually does not liberate hydrogen with most metals because it oxidises the hydrogen to water, producing nitrogen oxides instead depending on concentration and metal.

Concentrated nitric acid is a powerful oxidising agent. It oxidises non-metals such as carbon and sulphur to their oxides or oxy-acids and reacts with metals to give nitrates and nitrogen dioxide in many cases. Very dilute nitric acid may react with magnesium or manganese to liberate hydrogen, but such cases are exceptions.

items.note: Concentrated nitric acid oxidises copper, producing brown NO2 fumes.
Dilute nitric acid gives nitric oxide, which turns brown in air.

learn.title: Reactions with Metals, Non-metals and Aqua Regia

blocks.text: The products of reaction between nitric acid and metals depend on the concentration of acid and the reactivity of the metal. Concentrated nitric acid renders iron and aluminium passive by forming a protective oxide layer, preventing further reaction. This passivity is an important property in handling and storage.

Aqua regia is a freshly prepared mixture of concentrated hydrochloric acid and concentrated nitric acid in the ratio 3:1 by volume. It can dissolve noble metals like gold and platinum due to formation of highly reactive species. This illustrates the exceptional oxidising power associated with nitric acid in combination.

items: Passivity: protective oxide film on Fe or Al in concentrated HNO3 stops further attack.
Aqua regia must be freshly prepared and handled with extreme care.
Brown fumes of NO2 are a common observation with concentrated nitric acid reactions.
Reaction products vary; always specify concentration and conditions.

learn.title: Tests for Nitric Acid/Nitrates and Uses

blocks.text: The brown ring test is used to detect nitrate ions. To a solution containing nitrate, freshly prepared ferrous sulphate solution is added and concentrated sulphuric acid is poured carefully down the side of the test tube. A brown ring forms at the junction due to formation of a nitroso complex, indicating presence of nitrate.

Nitric acid is used in manufacture of fertilizers (such as ammonium nitrate), explosives, dyes and nitrates, and in etching and cleaning processes. Its oxidising nature makes it valuable in chemical industry, but also requires strict safety precautions during storage and use.

questions.prompt: Nitric acid is stored in dark bottles because it:
questions.explanation: Light causes nitric acid to decompose, forming NO2 which gives a yellow colour.
questions.commonMistake: The yellow colour is due to dissolved nitrogen dioxide.

questions.prompt: In the laboratory, nitric acid is prepared using:
questions.explanation: A nitrate salt heated with concentrated sulphuric acid yields nitric acid vapours.
questions.commonMistake: NaCl with conc. H2SO4 is used to prepare HCl, not HNO3.

questions.prompt: Brown fumes evolved when copper reacts with concentrated nitric acid are:
questions.explanation: Concentrated nitric acid oxidises copper and produces nitrogen dioxide, a brown gas.
questions.commonMistake: Dilute nitric acid may produce NO, which turns brown in air.

questions.prompt: Aqua regia is a mixture of concentrated HCl and concentrated HNO3 in the ratio:
questions.explanation: Aqua regia consists of three parts concentrated hydrochloric acid and one part concentrated nitric acid by volume.
questions.commonMistake: Remember the order: HCl is in larger proportion.

questions.prompt: The brown ring test is used to detect:
questions.explanation: Formation of a brown ring at the junction indicates presence of nitrate ions.
questions.commonMistake: Use freshly prepared FeSO4 solution for the test.

questions.prompt: Nitric acid usually does not liberate hydrogen with metals because it is:
questions.explanation: Nitric acid oxidises nascent hydrogen to water, so hydrogen gas is generally not evolved.
questions.commonMistake: Some exceptions exist with very dilute acid and specific metals.

questions.prompt: Iron becomes passive when treated with:
questions.explanation: A protective oxide layer forms on iron in concentrated nitric acid, preventing further reaction.
questions.commonMistake: Dilute nitric acid does not produce the same passivity effect.

questions.prompt: Industrial manufacture of nitric acid from ammonia is done by:
questions.explanation: The Ostwald process converts ammonia to nitric acid through catalytic oxidation steps.
questions.commonMistake: Haber process manufactures ammonia, not nitric acid.

questions.prompt: The yellow colour of old nitric acid is due to dissolved ________.
questions.explanation: Decomposition of nitric acid produces NO2, which imparts a yellow/brown colour.
questions.commonMistake: Write the correct name or formula (NO2).

questions.prompt: A mixture that can dissolve gold is called ________.
questions.explanation: Aqua regia is a powerful mixture of concentrated HCl and HNO3.
questions.commonMistake: Neither acid alone can dissolve gold under ordinary conditions.

questions.prompt: In the brown ring test, a brown ring forms at the junction due to a ________ complex.
questions.explanation: The brown ring is attributed to formation of a nitroso iron complex.
questions.commonMistake: Use freshly prepared ferrous sulphate for reliable results.

questions.prompt: Write the equation for laboratory preparation of nitric acid from potassium nitrate.
questions.explanation: Concentrated sulphuric acid displaces nitric acid from the nitrate on gentle heating.
questions.commonMistake: Use all-glass apparatus and controlled temperature.

questions.prompt: Why is the apparatus for preparing nitric acid made entirely of glass?
questions.answer: Nitric acid vapours are highly corrosive and attack materials like cork and rubber. An all-glass apparatus prevents damage and contamination during preparation.
questions.explanation: Material compatibility is important when handling reactive vapours.
questions.commonMistake: Mention corrosive nature of nitric acid vapours.

questions.prompt: State the observations when copper reacts with (i) concentrated nitric acid and (ii) dilute nitric acid.
questions.answer: (i) With concentrated nitric acid, brown fumes of nitrogen dioxide are evolved and a blue solution of copper nitrate is formed. (ii) With dilute nitric acid, nitric oxide gas is evolved which turns brown in air, and a blue solution of copper nitrate is formed.
questions.explanation: Products depend on acid concentration, though copper nitrate forms in both cases.
questions.commonMistake: Identify the nitrogen oxide correctly for each concentration.

questions.prompt: What is meant by passivity of iron in concentrated nitric acid?
questions.answer: When iron is treated with concentrated nitric acid, it becomes passive due to formation of a thin, protective oxide layer on its surface. This layer prevents further reaction between the acid and the metal.
questions.explanation: Passivity is a surface phenomenon that stops continued chemical attack.
questions.commonMistake: This effect occurs with concentrated, not dilute, nitric acid.

questions.prompt: Describe the brown ring test for nitrates with procedure and observation.
questions.answer: Take the nitrate solution in a test tube and add freshly prepared ferrous sulphate solution. Carefully pour concentrated sulphuric acid down the side of the tilted test tube so that it forms a separate layer below the solution. A brown ring appears at the junction of the two layers, indicating the presence of nitrate ions.
questions.explanation: The careful layering allows formation of the characteristic brown ring complex.
questions.commonMistake: Concentrated sulphuric acid must be added slowly along the side, not mixed vigorously.

questions.prompt: Explain why nitric acid is a strong oxidising agent and give two examples of its oxidising action.
questions.answer: Nitric acid readily decomposes to provide nascent oxygen or nitrogen oxides that accept electrons, enabling it to oxidise other substances. For example, concentrated nitric acid oxidises copper to copper nitrate while producing brown NO2 fumes, and it oxidises non-metals such as carbon to carbon dioxide (or sulphur to sulphuric acid under suitable conditions). In these reactions, nitric acid is reduced while the other substance is oxidised.
questions.explanation: Oxidising behaviour is evident from products formed and changes in reacting substances.
questions.commonMistake: Support the explanation with specific examples and observations.

questions.prompt: Outline the Ostwald process for the manufacture of nitric acid, including key steps and equations.
questions.answer: The Ostwald process manufactures nitric acid from ammonia in three main steps. (1) Catalytic oxidation: ammonia is oxidised by air in presence of platinum-rhodium catalyst at about 800°C to form nitric oxide: 4NH3 + 5O2 → 4NO + 6H2O. (2) Oxidation of nitric oxide: 2NO + O2 → 2NO2. (3) Absorption: nitrogen dioxide is absorbed in water in presence of oxygen to form nitric acid: 4NO2 + 2H2O + O2 → 4HNO3. The acid obtained is then concentrated as required.
questions.explanation: Sequential oxidation and absorption steps convert ammonia to nitric acid.
questions.commonMistake: Include catalyst/conditions where relevant and balance equations.

questions.prompt: A colourless sample of nitric acid turns yellow after being left in sunlight. Explain the change and suggest how to prevent it.
questions.answer: Nitric acid decomposes in presence of sunlight to form nitrogen dioxide, water and oxygen: 4HNO3 → 4NO2 + 2H2O + O2. The dissolved brown NO2 imparts a yellow colour to the acid. To prevent this, nitric acid should be stored in dark or brown glass bottles away from heat and light.
questions.explanation: Decomposition products cause the observed colour change.
questions.commonMistake: Link prevention directly to protection from light.

questions.prompt: Why is hydrogen gas generally not evolved when metals react with nitric acid, unlike with dilute hydrochloric acid?
questions.answer: Nitric acid is a strong oxidising agent. Any hydrogen initially formed is oxidised by nitric acid to water, while nitric acid itself is reduced to nitrogen oxides such as NO or NO2 depending on conditions. In contrast, dilute hydrochloric acid is not an oxidising agent in this way, so hydrogen gas is liberated with reactive metals.
questions.explanation: The oxidising nature of nitric acid changes the expected acid-metal reaction products.
questions.commonMistake: Mention the reduction products of nitric acid when explaining absence of hydrogen.

questions.prompt: A student adds concentrated nitric acid to iron filings and observes little reaction after an initial response. Explain the observation and how the iron can be made reactive again.
questions.answer: Concentrated nitric acid makes iron passive by forming a thin, adherent oxide layer on its surface. This protective layer prevents further contact between the acid and the metal, so the reaction appears to stop. The iron can be made active again by removing the oxide layer, for example by scratching or treating appropriately, after which it can react under suitable conditions.
questions.explanation: Passivity is due to surface protection, not lack of inherent reactivity of iron.
questions.commonMistake: Distinguish passivity in concentrated acid from normal reactivity in dilute acid.

questions.prompt: How would you distinguish between a nitrate solution and a chloride solution using chemical tests?
questions.answer: For the nitrate solution, perform the brown ring test: add freshly prepared FeSO4 solution and carefully pour concentrated H2SO4 along the side of the test tube; a brown ring at the junction indicates nitrate. For the chloride solution, add AgNO3 solution in presence of dilute nitric acid; a white precipitate of AgCl soluble in excess NH4OH confirms chloride. The different reagents and observations distinguish the two anions.
questions.explanation: Each anion has a characteristic confirmatory test.
questions.commonMistake: Use correct reagents and note the specific positive observations for each test.
